member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.HayateValueStringBuilder
member.summary: A zero-allocation, stack-only string builder in the ZString / Cosmos ValueStringBuilder shape: a ref struct whose character buffer is rented from , doubled when it grows, and handed back the moment materializes the result — the one and only allocation of a build.
member.remarks:
This type complements rather than replacing it. The transient "build → produce the string" flow (log lines, message formatting) runs here with no heap traffic beyond the final string; long-lived builders that cross methods or need pool observability stay on the pool. The builder never touches the HayateOP engine — is its pool — so it has no statistics, no validation and no capacity ceiling, just the raw fast path.
Appends follow ZString's shape and return void: the builder is a mutable ref struct, so chained calls like sb.Append(a).Append(b) would run on struct copies and lose their position state — call the methods in sequence instead.
Lifecycle. Rent with new (or using var, which disposes at the end of the block), append, and call ; the buffer returns to the pool right after the string is materialized, so the borrow ends at the call, exactly like . is idempotent, and a second on an already-materialized builder throws rather than reading a buffer that now belongs to someone else. Every member other than throws once the builder has ended.
Views. and hand out the current content without ending the borrow, but a view is invalidated by anything that moves the buffer (growth, is fine, growth is not) and must not outlive the builder — after or the span points into a pool buffer that the next renter owns.
This is a ref struct: the compiler keeps it on the stack, so it cannot be boxed, captured by a lambda, or held across an await — the misuse cases are compile-time errors, not runtime hazards. A thread-static fast path (ZString's thread cache, with its no-nesting rule) is a possible future enhancement and deliberately not part of this first version.

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.MemoryStreamPool
member.summary: A ready-to-use pool of instances, aligned with P89OP's MemoryStreamPool: borrowing costs one line, and using on the borrowed stream returns it.
member.remarks:
The pool is built on the ordinary HayateOP engine, configured the way a specialized stream pool wants it: nothing is pre-created, a miss inside the pool size is served by creating a stream on demand, and the two background features a stream pool has no use for (auto-scaling, eviction) are switched off — so an idle pool holds its streams and runs no timers. Validation stays on: it is what enforces the capacity window below, on every return.
Streams are created with bytes and may grow while borrowed; a stream that comes back with a capacity outside the / window is destroyed instead of being parked, so buffers never linger larger than the configuration allows. Returned streams are reset to empty (position and length zero) before the next borrow.
lets the borrower declare the capacity it needs up front. Declared sizes above the minimum are served by lazily created capacity tiers — one internal engine pool per bucket on the exponential ladder anchored at the minimum — so a mixed-size workload stops paying the grow ladder on every borrow and stops churning streams through grow-past-the-maximum-and-destroy: a tier accepts its declared size back even when that is above , because the buffer exists by declaration rather than by accidental growth. Each tier holds up to the pool's stream budget itself, so every declared size retains at most maxPoolSize streams.
Tightening the window clears the pool, matching P89OP: raising the minimum or lowering the maximum destroys every parked stream, because none of them can pass the new window; raising the minimum also retires the existing tiers so everything is recreated at the new size.

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.PooledMemoryStream
member.summary: A that knows the pool it came from: disposing it returns it to that pool instead of closing it, so a borrow/return pair can be written with using exactly as P89OP's PooledMemoryStream allows.
member.remarks:
Disposing a stream that sits in a hands it back through the pool's ordinary return path — validation, the capacity guard and the reset to an empty stream all behave exactly as for a manual Release — and the stream stays open: the buffer is kept alive for the next borrower, which is the whole point of pooling streams. The stream is closed for real only when the pool itself destroys it (a returned stream that failed validation — most commonly one that grew past the pool's maximum capacity — is destroyed, and the pool's destroy path calls the underlying ).
Disposal is once-per-borrow: a second of the same borrow is a no-op rather than a duplicate return, because returning the same object twice would let two borrowers share it later. After the pool has destroyed a stream, using it throws , like any closed stream.
A stream created directly (never handed out by a pool) owns nobody and behaves like an ordinary : disposing it closes it.

example.code: using var stream = MemoryStreamPool.Instance.GetObject(); stream.Write(payload, 0, payload.Length); // returned to the pool at the end of the block

member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.SharedStringBuilder
member.summary: One shared by everyone who wants one, guarded by a single lock — the thread-safe shared builder P89OP used to ship alongside its specialized pools.
member.remarks:
There is exactly one backing builder: acquiring it blocks every other acquirer until the holder disposes, which is the deliberate trade this type makes. Where a pool hands each borrower its own builder, this type hands every borrower the builder — zero per-use allocation beyond the resulting string, at the price of serialising all users behind one lock.
The lock boundary is multi-writer, single-holder: writes from one holder at a time are serialized, and the reader's snapshot is taken under the same lock, so no writer can interleave in the middle of a snapshot and no reader can observe a half-written buffer. Hold scopes briefly and never across an await; a long-held scope stalls every other user of the shared builder.
Disposal clears the builder and releases the lock, exactly once (a second is a no-op), so the next acquirer starts from an empty builder.

member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.StringBuilderPool.MinimumStringBuilderCapacity
member.summary: The capacity a builder is created with. Defaults to .
member.remarks: This is the creation capacity only: a builder's capacity never shrinks, so there is no minimum to enforce on the way back. member.name: P:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.StringBuilderPool.MaximumStringBuilderCapacity
member.summary: The maximum capacity a returned builder may have to be accepted back into the pool; larger builders are destroyed on return. Defaults to .
member.remarks: Lowering this value clears the pool: parked builders above the new maximum cannot pass it. Builders borrowed through remain covered by their tier's declared size, which parks them even above this maximum — declared capacity is what keeps a mixed-size workload from churning.

member.summary: Acquires a builder able to hold at least characters without growing, reserving the capacity up front so the borrow skips the grow ladder entirely.
member.param: The number of characters the borrowed builder must hold without growth; must be greater than zero.
member.returns: A pooled builder whose capacity is at least .
member.remarks: Requests within are served by the base tier exactly like . Anything larger routes to a lazily created capacity tier — the smallest bucket of the exponential ladder anchored at the minimum that covers the request — so repeated borrows of the same size reuse a parked builder instead of growing one from scratch every time, and a tier builder is parked on return even when its capacity exceeds . member.name: T:DotNetCore.HayateOP.Specialized.StringBuilderPoolPolicy
member.summary: The policy behind : creates builders at the configured capacity, guards the maximum capacity on the way back, and clears returned builders.
member.remarks: Each capacity tier the pool runs gets its own policy instance. The base tier uses tierCapacity = 0 and follows the pool's live minimum; a declared tier pins the capacity the tier serves, so the tier creates builders at that size and accepts them back even when the tier exceeds the pool's global maximum — the borrower declared the need, and parking the buffer is what keeps a mixed-size workload from destroying and recreating oversized builders on every use.
